stanzas: que la patria os contempla orgullosa,
que morir por la patria es vivir!
su poder y su orgullo ¿do es ido?
To combat run, men of Bayamo,
for the homeland looks on you with pride;
do not fear a glorious death,
for to die for the homeland is to live!
To live in chains is to live
Hear the sound of the bugle.
Hear the sound of the bugle.
Do not fear the fierce Iberians:
they are cowards, like every tyrant;
they cannot withstand the Cuban arm;
their empire has fallen for ever.
Free Cuba! Spain has died now;
its power and its pride, where have they gone?
Hear the sound of the bugle,
as brave men we know how to triumph!
at the terrible blast of the cannon;
hear the sound of the bugle,

notes: line 1.1: 'Bayameses': the people of Bayamo, the town in eastern Cuba where the song was first sung (1868).
lines 2.4, 4.4, 6.4: 'valientes' is read as an address ('brave ones'); it can also be taken as 'run bravely'.
line 3.4: the text has 'calló' ('fell silent'), here read as 'cayó' ('fell'), which the sense requires; literally 'their empire has fallen silent for ever'.
line 4.2: '¿do es ido?' is an archaic 'where has it gone?'.
